before.name: Full Richardson
before.overview: Up a distinct couloir on the North Face: two WI2/3 steps and about 300 ft of moderate snow lead to the 30m crux, steep aerated ice with poor gear but great axe sticks, behaving more like alpine than water ice. A picket above the curtain makes the belay; lacking one, use ice screws lower down. Moderate snow in the bowl follows, around 600 feet to the summit; mind avalanche conditions. To skip the upper pitches, go right and descend. Snow steepens under the summit block and may be loose at the very top; a short crumbly mixed ramp (M3) on the right avoids it. Rappel west-northwest from the top, downclimb the NW ridge to a north-facing slope, then head east to your gear at the couloir base.
before.detailed_rack: Screws (with stubbies) and pickets.
before.approach: The line follows a conspicuous gully in Broken Top's north face; some of the ice is visible from the bottom of it. Two short steps of ice or snow, depending on the season, come first, then moderate snow leads up the couloir. Watch the snow stability here and check the avalanche forecast.
before.descent_text: From the summit, rappel to the west-northwest, then downclimb the northwest ridge to a north-facing slope and traverse east back to the gear left at the foot of the couloir. Parties who want to skip the summit pitches can also traverse right and descend earlier.

before.name: High Noon
before.detailed_rack: Take pickets and possibly passive gear, but expect crumbly rock that is bad even for Oregon.
before.location: Up the south face directly, beginning on the snowfield dividing it.

before.name: Black Spider - Fric-Amos
before.overview: On Hood's east face, the Black Spider wall's left flank has 3 ice and mixed pitches, with snowfields and gullies between them. P1: steep ice drip left on the lowest rock band, sunny and not always formed; a variation takes the slim ice gully at the band's right end. P2, the key pitch: a full 60m of it from the snowfield's upper left corner. Snow gully above, toward the rock band upper right. P3: a brief ice step right of the band onto upper snow; variations may exist. The last gully veers left and joins Wyeast Ridge just before the summit. All routes here get morning sun; the first-pitch variation and the second pitch are partly shaded. Pick a cold day; watch overhead hazard.
before.detailed_rack: Eight to ten screws, stubbies among them, a compact rock rack and a few pitons.
before.approach: The Black Spider is reached from Timberline, from the Cooper Spur side, or from the Meadows ski area. From Timberline, follow the South Side approach, then cross the White River Glacier and continue around to the foot of the wall. The route starts on the left side of the wall, after crossing the bergschrund at the head of the Newton Clark Glacier. Cold, early starts keep the face out of the sun and away from overhead hazard.
before.location: Mt. Hood east face, Black Spider wall, left half of the amphitheater. Foot at 10,000 feet, past the bergschrund high on the Newton Clark glacier.

before.name: Black Spider - Three Little Monkeys (Burkhardt-Getlin)
before.overview: Six pitches, with steep snow on P6 up to the ridge of the summit. P1 (M3 WI4+): the first crux, just above the ground, is a brittle, free-standing pillar followed by fussy mixed moves. P2 (M4/5 X): go straight up if the ice links up; the party instead went right, across loose, steep snow, to a chimney of vertical mud that stands out. P3 goes left to a small WI3- chimney flow; P4 climbs it, veering right; P5 turns the corner rightward and goes up to the spine under a spire.
before.detailed_rack: Pins, Specters, pickets, cams and screws.
before.approach: The line is the ice streak between the Elder-Russel and Fric-Amos routes, just left of the toe at the centre of the Black Spider wall. The usual way in is from Timberline, following the South Side approach, crossing the White River Glacier and continuing around to the foot of the wall, then crossing the bergschrund to reach the start.
before.name_search: black spider three 3 little monkeys burkhardt getlin

before.name: Wy'East
before.overview: Start at Timberline Lodge, take the climbers trail to the Palmer lift top, then head east over the glacier called White River; roping up is wise among the crevasses. Climb the moraine to the ridge, then to a rock outcrop. Skirt the rocks on their right and ascend a 40 degree chute, returning to the ridge about 400 feet higher; this is the top of Steel Cliffs, with Devils Kitchen beneath. The somewhat exposed ridge leads to a snow ramp leaning right, or exposed rock, then a small downclimb, fairly easy if frozen. Angle up and right below a big rock formation, then a 50 to 55 degree chute gains the crest and summit. Late season: heavy rockfall, rotten rock, harder route finding.
before.detailed_rack: Pickets, ice axe, an extra tool, crampons and a helmet.
before.approach: Start at Timberline Lodge and follow the boot-packed path to the upper terminal of the Palmer lift. Head east across the White River Glacier, roped because of crevasses, and climb the moraine to reach the ridge.
before.descent_text: Descend by the standard South Side route back to Timberline Lodge.

op.name: East Face aka "Brainless Child" (Tyler Adams Memorial Route)

before.name: East Face aka "Brainless Child" (Tyler Adams Memorial Route)
before.overview: Mt. Thielsen's east face gets sun from dawn to mid-afternoon; ice pellets, chunks and rocks came down, and screws barely worked while rock gear was good but scarce. Opening pitch (about 65m, probably 5.9) trends left up a buttress of rock onto the ice, on solid rock with decent pro. Gully ice goes about WI3+, then soft deteriorating WI4+ including a roughly 10m vertical stretch. The fourth pitch is rotten ice with 10m lacking any pro. Two snow gully pitches precede the couloir higher up, simul-climbed to the ridge under the summit.
before.detailed_rack: Snow pickets, screws, cams. One party brought eight screws, cams up to nearly #3, assorted wires, KBs, LAs, beaks, and Specters, which proved very handy.
before.approach: Follow the Thielsen Trail to its junction with the Pacific Crest Trail, then leave the trail and contour around the west and north faces to the saddle between the north and east faces. The start of the route is a short way beyond the saddle. The east face gets early sun. The mountain has avalanche, rockfall and icefall hazards, so check the avalanche forecast.
before.name_search: east face aka brainless child tyler adams memorial route rte

before.name: Western Gulch
before.detailed_rack: Crampons, tools, slings, one or two pickets, and screws; add cams sized 1-2' for the NW Arete.
before.approach: Follow the hiker's route toward the Pacific Crest Trail, or the gully just north of it if snow and conditions favour that. At the PCT crossing, look for the west-facing snow apron with avalanche-bent trees; the gully starts near its upper right edge. The apron is avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast, and plan to finish before the sun reaches the summit pinnacle, when rock and ice come down the gully.

before.name: Exegesis
before.overview: Walk about 2.5 miles of trail from the trailhead at Hurricane Creek to a creek crossing, move to the east bank, then continue 2.5 miles more along Thorp Creek. Begin the steep part below the NNE face at a big outcrop right of center, and head straight up between rock towers and snow slopes reaching 70 degrees. Higher, move right to the NW ridge and the summit ridge. There are no permanent belay or rappel stations. Descend the NW ridge and the Hurricane Creek Trail. Prefer snow when it is stable and hides the rock, rock when snow is unstable and the rock bare. Move light and fast, as snow softens by mid to late morning; soloing might be safest.
before.detailed_rack: Expect little rock protection, only passive pieces at most. Late winter or early spring, leave screws behind, though one short screw might be a safeguard. The lower slopes offer many picket placements.

before.name: Devil's Kitchen Headwall (DKH) - Left Variation
before.detailed_rack: Seems best in late winter or early spring. Lean conditions can be sketchy, with short screws and thin pins likely the only pro. With fat ice and consolidated snow above, take pickets and medium-length screws.
before.approach: From Timberline Lodge, hike uphill to the Devil's Kitchen crater. The route climbs the long couloir splitting the middle of the Devil's Kitchen Headwall: go up the snow and debris slope below the headwall into the couloir's entrance, then steep snow to the first ice step.
before.name_search: devils kitchen headwall dkh left lt variation var

before.name: Devil's Kitchen Headwall (DKH) - Right Variation
before.overview: This option, known as V2, sits beside the standard left-hand DKH route (V1) and is a more interesting approach to the Wyeast route's best terrain. It sits in the corner formed by the headwall and Steel Cliffs, and starts on moderate snow. A fork about halfway has a left branch that dead-ends, which makes a possible belay point below the steeper upper section. Take the right branch, roughly straight up, through a steep last bit onto the Steel Cliffs' top, then choose a path through the upper Wyeast route's gendarmes to the summit.
before.detailed_rack: Kit varies with conditions: 2-3 pickets, ice screws. Early June brought rotten ice-snow on the upper steepening, and firm snow lower, in the runnels.
before.approach: From Timberline Lodge, hike uphill to the Devil's Kitchen crater. The route is tucked into the angle where the headwall above the Devil's Kitchen runs into the Steel Cliffs, and begins on moderate snow.
before.name_search: devils kitchen headwall dkh right rt variation var

before.name: East Crater Wall (DKH V4)
before.detailed_rack: Fatal if you fall unarrested on the ridge. A slip lower could end in the Devils Kitchen Fumerol, over 100 feet deep with poisonous fumes. Pickets hold only where the surface is consolidated, so soloing unprotected may be the sole option.
before.approach: Take the standard South Side approach from Timberline Lodge up to the Devil's Kitchen. In the bowl, find the debris cone on the climber's right, then look up toward the ridge: the last chute before the steeper Steel Cliffs is the route, and it leads to the Wy'East ridge. Small crevasses can lie at the base. The Wy'East finish above is exposed and avalanche-prone, so check the avalanche forecast.

before.name: Flying Buttress (DKH V3)
before.overview: This variant has milder ice than the standard lines and finishes on the upper Wyeast route, with its steep snow crux and exposed gendarme. Climb easy ice or moderate snow in the gully toward an apparent dead-end headwall. Near its top, go right up an obvious snow ramp to the Wyeast ridge crest, then left along it past a small saddle where DKH V2 joins and a short traverse that may be the crux. Moderate to steep, exposed snow follows, easing toward the summit.
before.detailed_rack: Bring two tools, or one tool and an axe, plus pickets and a few ice screws if pitching.
before.approach: From Timberline Lodge, hike to the Devil's Kitchen. Keep the big fumarole on your right, then slant up and to the right across the basin to the base of the third major couloir of the headwall, counting from the left.

before.name: Icefall Chute (Boy Scouts Chute)
before.approach: Follow the South Side route from Timberline Lodge to the Hogsback. Head uphill, angling slightly right but staying left of the Pearly Gates, and cross the large bergschrund below the chute. The narrow chute starts just left of the Left Pearly Gate. Icefall is the main worry early in the season and rockfall later. Avalanche gear may be warranted, so check the avalanche forecast.
before.descent_text: Descend by whichever is safest, typically Old Chute or the Pearly Gates.

before.name: Men of Steel
before.overview: Meanders through connected gullies up the Steel Cliff's main face at a modest grade. At the top it joins the Wy'East route toward the summit; alternatively downclimb to Devil's Kitchen in several ways. Start in a gully right of the big rock blob at the base (another start enters from the left). Above the blob, gullies lead up and left to the crater rim past several steeper ice steps. The last steep step before the ridge could be the crux, with a left exit perhaps best; knowledge of this route is limited. Wait for a thick, solid rime layer on the cliff. Gear may be scarce.
before.approach: From Timberline Lodge, hike uphill to the Devil's Kitchen. The route is in the middle of the Steel Cliff, which rises above the Devil's Kitchen on its east side.
before.descent_text: The top joins the Wy'East route and its variations, which lead to the summit. Alternatively, descend to the Devil's Kitchen by a variation such as the Flying Buttress or East Crater Wall.

before.name: Steel Cliff South Face
before.overview: Aim for the foot of the first chute, coming from the Palmer snowfield over the glacier and heading toward the Wy'east ridge. Climb the snow slope while watching for hazards falling from the cliffs. At the cliffs, bear left over a small iced band; many ice paths exist. Pitched out it makes two 30m pitches. Continue up the second chute to the top of an apparent small cliff or crossing ridge, then take the easiest way over the Wy'east ridge on climber's right and finish on the usual Wy'east line. A fine alternative to steeper, shorter south-side lines: it gets onto steeper ground lower yet stays moderate. The stated grade feels slightly light.
before.approach: Cross the White River Glacier from the Palmer Snowfield toward the Wy'East ridge to reach the obvious foot of the first chute.
before.descent_text: Follow the standard Wy'East route down.

before.name: North Face Couloir
before.overview: Middle of three routes up the north side of South Sister. That wall is about 1000 feet tall and averages 45 degrees, with steeper steps. A steep couloir is used to pass the upper rock bands. Early season, with snow and ice, is best.
before.detailed_rack: Two tools; add screws and pickets for roped climbing.
before.approach: The north side has a long approach, reached either by Green Lakes and the Prouty Glacier from the south, or by Pole Creek from the north. Early in the season it can be skied. A bivy on the Skinner Glacier below the face makes it a good two-day trip. This is the middle of the three north-face routes.
before.descent_text: Descend the North Ridge back to your camp, or carry your gear over the summit and go down the South Side.

op.name: North Face of the Northwest Ridge

before.name: North Face of the Northwest Ridge
before.fa: David Byrne, Tim Scott, Derek Castonguay, 2011
before.overview: Rightmost of three routes up the north side of South Sister; that wall is about 1000 feet tall and averages 45 degrees with steeper steps. A gap in the rock band, reached past an ice step, opens the upper face. Early season with abundant snow is best. Variation: above the gap, trend up and left to the final rock bands near the crater rim, which can be rotten if snowless; then go up and right to reach the Northwest Ridge for roughly its final 300 feet.
before.detailed_rack: Two tools; screws and pickets if roped.
before.approach: This is the rightmost of the three north-face routes and is identified by a gap in the rock band. The approach is long, reached either by Green Lakes and the Prouty Glacier from the south, or by Pole Creek from the north. Camp on the Skinner Glacier at the foot of the face.
before.descent_text: Descend the North Ridge back to your camp, or continue over the summit and go down the South Side.
before.name_search: north face of the northwest nw ridge rdg

before.name: Silver Couloir
before.fa: Gerald Calbaum, Nick Doge, Gary Kirk, 1973
before.overview: Takes the leftmost couloir on the north face, climbed straight up from the top of the Skinner Glacier. It should only be attempted when firmly frozen, as falling rock and avalanches are a danger otherwise.
before.detailed_rack: Carry two tools; roped parties add screws and pickets.
before.approach: This is the leftmost of the three north-face routes. The approach is long, reached either by Green Lakes and the Prouty Glacier from the south, or by Pole Creek from the north; early in the season it can be skied. Camp on the Skinner Glacier at the foot of the face and treat it as a two-day trip.
before.descent_text: Descend the North Ridge back to your camp, or carry your gear over the summit and go down the South Side.

before.name: Cathedral Ramp
before.overview: P1 (55m) offers two options. Left: fun standard WI3 to the upper ramp, steeper than it looks. Right: a brief mixed-ice step off the glacier and a long icy traverse merging left. Next, cut far left into the snow gully seen from the base; a leader going far up the ramp can reach the top of the cleaver on the North Face with one more pitch. P2 (60m): snow, then ice/mixed, then right on loose dry rock exposed to the left, to the top of The Pencil. P3 (60m): leftward past the corner across snow and simple rock, aiming for the top of Right Gully. P4 (30m): easy snow, crumbly rock. Finish with ~500 vertical feet on snow, ice and gentle mixed ground, also used by Ravine, The Pencil and Right Gully.
before.detailed_rack: Nuts (a small set), a handful of cams from 0.4 to 1, and screws, stubbies among them. Pitons might help; none were placed in 2021.
before.approach: The route is on the cleaver's western flank at the head of the Eliot Glacier. From the Tilly Jane Hut, follow trails onto the moraine ridge bordering the glacier's east edge, then go up onto the glacier and continue up the upper Eliot Glacier. Another option is to come in sideways from the upper end of the Sunshine Route.
before.location: North Face Cleaver's west face, from about 10,000 feet up.

before.name: Eliot Glacier Headwall
before.detailed_rack: Bring two tools (or a short axe plus a tool), five to eight screws and a couple of pickets.
before.approach: From the Cloud Cap and Tilly Jane side, follow the trail past the Tilly Jane cabin to the Cooper Spur trail, then watch for a large cairn marking a use trail that drops to the Eliot Glacier. Cross the lower moraine to the west side of the glacier, then work up to the foot of the headwall, crossing crevasses on bridges where you can. Another way in is from the summit side by the Sunshine route to Queen's Chair, then a traverse into the headwall.
before.descent_text: Descend the Sunshine route or a south side route.
before.sun: In shade all day in October

before.name: North Face Left Gully
before.overview: The crux is the opening ice pitch, longer and harder than any in the Right Gully, forming anywhere within WI3-4; belay beneath it after crossing the bergshrund. Above, the route heads straight to Mt Hood's summit on steep snow with now and then an easy ice step. Gear placements are very hard to find past that pitch, so climbers should be at ease moving together or unroped on moderate alpine ground.
before.detailed_rack: Screws, pickets, and perhaps a little rock gear.
before.approach: Most parties set out at Tilly Jane or Cloud Cap and follow the paths to the moraine ridge bordering the Eliot Glacier's east edge, then cross the glacier to the foot of the North Face. The bergschrund is crossed and a belay set below the first pitch of ice.
before.descent_text: The descent depends on where the car is. To return to Tilly Jane, descend Cooper Spur or the Sunshine Route, both on steep snow; the Sunshine Route has bergschrunds. To return to Timberline, take the South Side route.
before.name_search: north face left lt gully gulley

before.name: North Face Right Gully
before.fa: Mark Weygant, Arthur Emmons, Orville Emmons, 1928
before.overview: Counted among the peak's finest lines; timing is the crux, since it must be found in shape; then it gives superb ice pitches reaching WI4. Start at the Cloud Cap or Tilly Jane campground and follow marked climber paths through trees to the ridge forming lower Cooper Spur. A cairn on the right marks the way down onto the glacier. Keep left on the ice, watching for seracs and crevasses, and angle right near the Eliot headwall. Two couloirs there slant up leftward; the right one usually has more vertical ice (3-4 vertical sections, first two hardest). The left starts vertical, then is mostly snow. Two ways down are Cooper Spur and Sunshine; the south side also works if cars are shuttled.
before.detailed_rack: A 60m rope, pickets, and 6-8 short screws.
before.approach: Start from the Tilly Jane or Cloud Cap campgrounds and follow climbers' trails through the trees. Above treeline, climb the lower Cooper Spur ridge until a cairn on the right marks the path down onto the Eliot Glacier. Cross the glacier along its left side, watching for seracs and crevasses, and move right as you near the headwall. The right gully is the right-hand of two couloirs angling up and left on the headwall's right side.
before.descent_text: Descend Cooper Spur or the Sunshine route back to the start, or go down the south side and arrange a car shuttle.
before.name_search: north face right rt gully gulley

before.name: Ravine
before.overview: About 50 m of ice makes one full pitch, rising from easy ice through a steep, slightly overhanging bulge (the crux, with poor footholds) to a snow couloir. The flow is thick and protects well with ice gear; the only rock placements were a #1 Camalot and a #3 Metolius. In the couloir, gentler than when viewed from Cathedral ridge, belay off snow pickets. Then move right and over, either soloing, simul soloing or belaying from the top, and merge into the North Face route to the summit.
before.detailed_rack: A red BD Camalot in size #1, a Metolius in size #3 (orange), 2-4 pickets, and ice screws (between 5 and 10, by comfort).
before.approach: The route sits to the right of Cathedral Spire. Reach it from the Tilly Jane Hut side by going onto the Eliot Glacier from the lateral moraine, then either traverse toward Cathedral Spire below the Eliot headwall or hike up the glacier past the bergschrund.

before.name: East Buttress
before.overview: Direct line over varied terrain from 7400 feet to roughly 9800 ft. The lower part opens with an ice pillar at the toe, probably the crux (snow ramps substitute if it is not formed), then skirts a big buttress on the right, edges left to the crest, scrambles, and follows the narrowing crest across a gendarme to tower number two, which sits over the notch. Rappelling 60m reaches that notch, near 8700 ft; from there the upper part runs up an obvious gully of mixed and icy terrain, then ramps through towers, ending on the NE bench of the pinnacle on the summit, which the Theyer Headwall line and the couloir at 11 o'clock also reach.
before.detailed_rack: Ice screws, cams (one set), nuts and pitons.
before.approach: Start from the Pole Creek trailhead and go up the Soap Creek drainage to the foot of the buttress, which projects east from the summit. The approach is straightforward in winter and can be done on skis.
before.descent_text: Descend by the South Ridge route, the Southwest Ridge, or the early-morning couloir.

before.name: KIDS
before.overview: Follows the short dagger in the bowl at lower right of the Thayer headwall. It rarely reaches the ground; a water-ice core is usually coated with thick sun-baked alpine ice. Screws hold poorly here, and the chute above gets wind-loaded and spindrifted. Past the steep section, a further 20m ramp of AI3 guards the upper snowfield, where the usual headwall line (M3) begins.
before.approach: The route is a short ice dagger in the lower right bowl of the Thayer Glacier headwall, on the east side of North Sister. Start at the Pole Creek trailhead, leave the trail and head east toward the east side of the mountain to the Thayer Glacier.

before.name: Thayer Glacier Headwall
before.overview: A thinly documented line known mainly from a secondhand report. It looks very dangerous, with exposure to both falling rock and avalanches.
before.approach: Start at the Pole Creek trailhead, leave the trail and head east toward the east side of North Sister, continuing until you reach the Thayer Glacier. Once on the glacier, choose one of the gullies; the centre one is the most direct.
before.descent_text: Retrace your route down, or go down the standard route.

before.name: Cathedral Ridge
before.overview: A little-used route because the walk in is long and the ridge itself holds little interest. The lower ridge is a tiring slog over scree, and the top part is firm steep snow or more scree. Wandering off line low down can put you onto scrambling ground of class 3 or 4.
before.detailed_rack: Slings for horns, a pair of pickets and a couple of shorter screws.

before.name: Leuthold Couloir
before.approach: From Timberline Lodge, ride or climb the Palmer lift and traverse upward to Illumination Saddle, which lies between Illumination Rock and Castle Crags. Cross the saddle and drop onto the Reid Glacier, then traverse toward Yocum Ridge, going by a number of couloirs on your right, until you reach the steep wall of the ridge. Turn right into Leuthold Couloir; starting up too early leads onto the Reid Glacier Headwall instead. The slopes are crevassed and avalanche-prone, so check the avalanche forecast.

before.name: Reid Glacier Headwall
before.fa: Gordon Facer, Marshall Cronyn, R.J. Corruccini, 1938
before.overview: A long, committing line. Depending on variation (probably half a dozen are established), expect 4 to 7 ice steps, from 10 feet up to nearly 40 higher on. The steps are not hard for ice but likely beyond single-axe ability, so two tools are advisable. Route finding is the main difficulty: parties have been stuck among the upper towers, mostly by drifting south (climber's right) into dead-ends at the jagged rim of the west. If unfamiliar, pick a day of good visibility, and go left when unsure. Storms hit the west face; rime above the headwall sheds as ice avalanches, so it can be a bowling alley.
before.detailed_rack: Ordinary alpine ice kit otherwise: screws (a handful), pickets (two or three), plus draws in single and double lengths. Ice is plentiful but not always where wanted. Falls are unlikely for able climbers and rime sheds, so a running belay saves time.
before.approach: From Timberline Lodge, cross the top of the Zigzag Glacier from the Palmer lift to the saddle between Illumination Rock and the main peak. The Reid Glacier lies below to the northwest with Yocum Ridge opposite. Stop short of the lowest rock cleaver below Yocum Ridge and turn up to the foot of the headwall. Rime above the headwall can avalanche into the couloirs, so check the avalanche forecast.
before.descent_text: Descend by the Old Chute, an easy ramp from the knife-edge rim into the crater.

before.name: Sandy Glacier Headwall
before.fa: Fred Ayers, Keith Petrie, Dave Hitchcock, Don McKay, 1956
before.overview: Reached from Illumination Saddle by dropping to the neighbouring glacier and skirting around the foot of Yocum Ridge. The route then climbs the glacier named for it and its headwall, where slopes reach about 50 degrees. Both rockfall and avalanches threaten the way.
before.detailed_rack: Pickets, ice axe, an optional ice tool, and the rope, harness and ascenders or prussiks needed for glacier travel.
before.approach: Start at Timberline Lodge, climb past the lifts to Illumination Saddle, then head for Yocum Ridge. Skip Leuthold Couloir and descend close to the ridge to avoid Reid Glacier crevasses, then cross over Yocum Ridge at a low point to the upper Sandy Glacier and traverse to the headwall on its far north side. Many parties split it into two days by camping at the saddle.

before.name: Yocum Ridge
before.fa: Beckey, Scheiblehner, 1959; Young, Hiatt (via First Gendarme), 1972
before.detailed_rack: Rime makes gear finicky: 4-6 screws, 2-4 pickets, plus a few nuts, some pitons and a few cams, and skill with runouts and improvised anchors.
before.approach: Start at Timberline Lodge and climb to Illumination Saddle. Drop from the saddle onto the Reid Glacier and cross it to the start of the ridge.
before.descent_text: Descend Leuthold Couloir, or go over the summit and down a standard South Side route.

before.name: Northwest Arete
before.overview: Big blocks abound, with excellent hand jams and secure footholds. Some sections overhang, and the exposure is truly spicy. Cracks for gear are everywhere.
before.detailed_rack: Bring big pieces in addition to an alpine rack.
before.approach: Take the Mount Thielsen trail from the trailhead to the Pacific Crest Trail junction, then follow the well-used climbers path up toward the summit horn. Where the fourth-class trail nears the summit pinnacle, bear left rather than right and walk clockwise around the base of the pinnacle until the ledge ends at a cliff. A small to medium ledge there serves as the belay stance at the start of the arete.

before.name: Northeast Buttress (McLaughlin Memorial Route)
before.detailed_rack: Alpine rack of cams and nuts, tri-cams, Spectres, pitons and many double-length slings; long pins or Spectres and a hammer for the headwall; screws if in season.
before.approach: From the Howlock Mountain trailhead at the north end of Diamond Lake, take the Howlock Mountain trail to a junction and turn right onto the Thielsen Creek trail. At its junction with the Pacific Crest Trail, continue straight up the Thielsen Creek drainage toward the remnants of the old glacier. The route starts on the east side of the former glacier at the foot of the northeast buttress, with easy slabs below a system of right-facing dihedrals.
before.descent_text: Finish by scrambling the summit block by its regular south line, then descend the West Ridge. Getting back depends on whether a car or bikes were left at the Mt. Thielsen trailhead or the party walked in from Diamond Lake.
before.name_search: northeast ne buttress mclaughlin memorial route rte

before.name: East Ridge
before.overview: A well-established trail leads from the parking lot, meeting the PCT after 1.1 miles. Continue on the climbers trail past a second PCT junction (heading north) by staying straight. About 3 miles of good flowing trail precede the technical ground, where rocky footing, big step-ups and big drops lead to the East Ridge. Plod up the ridge to the last 600ft, a scree (or snow) slope ending at a large, pointed summit.
pro_tips: White dots and arrows are painted on the rock through the maze section; they stop about 250 ft below the top, so follow the ridge to the summit.
Roughly two miles in the middle are nearly flat, so the steep part comes late; start early to be off the loose upper mountain in daylight.
In early July a snowfield below the summit gave a glissade descent, but it ends well away from the trail; check where it lands.
watch_out: A canal crossing near the start has no bridge; in early July it is crossed on logs.
In July the tread fades in the upper scree and braids; pick your own line and watch for painted marks.
In early July bugs are bad below treeline and ease higher up.
before.approach: From the trailhead parking lot a good trail runs about a mile to the first Pacific Crest Trail junction. Stay on the McLoughlin climbers trail, go straight past a second PCT junction that leads north, and follow smooth trail for a few miles before the footing turns rocky, with large step-ups. The well-worn trail leads to the East Ridge itself, and the final slope to the pointed summit is scree or snow. The trailhead charges a fee and has no camping.

October.reason: By late October snow can lie on the upper trail, though it stays a trail hike in good weather.

before.name: Pete's Point
before.overview: A simple snow couloir on Pete's Point's north face, mostly a side trip when hiking in the Wallowas. Steepness is maybe 45 degrees over 750 feet. At 9695 ft, the summit ranks eleventh in elevation among Oregon's high points.
before.detailed_rack: For a roped ascent, add a couple of screws and pickets. Rockfall is possible.
before.approach: The trip starts at the Wallowa Lake trailhead, where the East Fork Wallowa River Trail (number 1804) climbs through forest, then meadows and beaver ponds, passing Rogers Lake before reaching Aneroid Lake roughly six miles in. Pete's Point sits above the lake between Tenderfoot Pass and Polaris Pass, and the route is the snow couloir on its north face. Carry an ice axe for the couloir; rockfall is possible.

before.name: Peking
before.location: Left of the parallel crack systems on the right side of Red Wall, ideologically left of Moscow

fill.overview: A straight line up the west side of Mount Jefferson to the summit pinnacle. The lower ridge is moderate snow; the pinnacle is sound rock. Protection is rarely needed until the pinnacle, so most parties carry a few pickets or screws for the snow and a light rack of nuts and slings for the top. The face holds shade well into the morning.
fill.approach: Reached from the west off the Pacific Crest Trail, starting from either the Pamelia Lake or the Woodpecker Ridge trailhead. The walk in is long; check which permit applies to the trailhead you choose.
fill.descent_text: Reverse the ridge, or traverse north around the pinnacle to its east side and downclimb loose fourth-class rock from there. Rockfall is common.
